new_statements.quote: Le [ngbàkà mānzā], comme beaucoup de langues centrafricaines, est une langue à tons. L'analyse du corpus a permis de constater que cette langue compte cinq registres tonals, repartis en deux types : les tons ponctuels et les tons modulés. [...] Trois tons ponctuels sont attestés [...] Il s'agit du ton haut (Th), du ton moyen (Tm) et du ton bas (Tb). [p. 88] ... Les noms d'emprunt subissent de variation suprasegmentale lors du processus de leur intégration : l'accent dans la langue source devient le ton haut (th) ou le ton haut-bas (thb) en [ngbàkà mānzā]. [...] La syllabe accentuée du nom d'emprunt, si elle est en position frontale ou médiane, porte le ton haut [...]. Mais au cas où elle se situe en position finale ou bien si elle est monosyllabique, elle porte le ton modulé haut-bas. [pp. 210-211]
new_statements.translation: Ngbaka Manza, like many Central African languages, is a tone language. Analysis of the corpus shows that the language has five tonal registers of two types, level and contour tones. [...] Three level tones are attested: high, mid and low. ... Loan nouns undergo suprasegmental change during integration: the stress of the source language becomes high tone or high-low tone in Ngbaka Manza. [...] The stressed syllable of the loan noun, if initial or medial, carries high tone; if it is final or the word is monosyllabic, it carries the falling high-low tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is described as tonal (H, M, L level tones plus HL and LH contours, all lexically/grammatically contrastive); the description contains no word-stress or accent rule. Stress is mentioned only as a property of donor languages that is reinterpreted as H (or final HL) tone in loans, i.e. the author treats Ngbaka Manza prosody as purely tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; only the loanword tone-assignment rule (non-final stressed syllable -> H, final/monosyllabic -> HL).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on isolated lexical items (proverb corpus and lexicon); intonation mentioned only in the orthography/punctuation chapter (question = rising, exclamation = falling).
new_statements.identity_note: Selezilo describes the Ngbaka Manza of Bogangolo (Ombella-Mpoko, CAR), i.e. ngba1287 / ISO ngg proper; not to be confused with Ngbaka Minagende (nga, DRC) or Ngbaka Ma'bo (nbm), which HAL and Glottolog name lists conflate.

new_statements.quote: Le ngbaka-manza, comme beaucoup de langues centrafricaines, est une langue à tons. L'analyse de notre corpus nous fait observer que le parler ngbaka-manza compte sept registres tonals, repartis en deux types : les tons ponctuels et les tons modulés. [...] Trois tons ponctuels sont attestés en ngbaka-manza. Il s'agit de ton haut (Th), ton moyen (Tm) et ton bas (Tb). [p. 80] [...] Quatre tons modulés sont attestés en ngbaka-manza. Il s'agit de ton haut-bas (Thb), ton haut-moyen (Thm), ton moyen-haut (Tmh) et ton bas-haut (Tbh). [p. 82]
new_statements.translation: Ngbaka-Manza, like many Central African languages, is a tone language. Analysis of our corpus shows us that the Ngbaka-Manza variety has seven tonal registers, divided into two types: level tones and contour tones. [...] Three level tones are attested in Ngbaka-Manza: high tone (Th), mid tone (Tm) and low tone (Tb). [...] Four contour tones are attested in Ngbaka-Manza: high-low (Thb), high-mid (Thm), mid-high (Tmh) and low-high (Tbh).

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same variety (Bogangolo), earlier and shorter (213 pp.) text of the thesis whose 2008 HAL version (504 pp.) supplies the existing statement. Both say Ngbaka Manza is a tone language and neither describes word stress, so the reading 'tone language, no stress statement' stands. Detail differing between the two versions concerns tone, not stress: 2006 counts seven registers (H M L + HL HM MH LH), 2008 counts five (H M L + HL LH).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical tone language (3 level tones H, M, L and, in this 2006 text, 4 contours HL, HM, MH, LH; tone schemes for mono- to quadrisyllabic words in §III.4). The thesis has no section on accent/stress: the words 'accent'/'accentué' do not occur anywhere in the text layer (the only 'acce-' hits are 'accepter' and 'acceptation'), and the only prosodic statement is that tone is 'généralement classé parmi les faits prosodiques.. une hauteur mélodique suprasegmentale utilisée de manière distinctive' (p. 79, PDF p. 86). No claim about word stress is made.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; unlike the 2008 HAL version, this 2006 text has no loanword chapter, so the 'source-language accent becomes H or HL tone' remark of the 2008 version (pp. 210-211) is absent here
new_statements.identity_note: Both Selezilo texts describe the Ngbaka Manza of Bogangolo (Ombella-M'Poko, Central African Republic); the 2006 title spells the language 'Ngbaka-Manza'. Blühberger's survey (abstract) treats Ngbaka Manza as a homogeneous unit distinct from Ngbaka Minagende, with partial intelligibility with Ali, Manza and Gbanu; it does not single out the Bogangolo variety.

sources.locator: §3.1 p. 88 (PDF p. 89); loanword chapter pp. 210-211 (PDF pp. 211-212)
sources.note: Phonology part (pp. 36-153) has chapters on vowels, consonants, 'Le système tonal' (pp. 88-94: three level tones H, M, L plus contours HL, LH, with minimal pairs) and syllable/tone-scheme distribution (pp. 113-118); there is no accent/stress section and no statement about word stress. 'Accent' appears only in the loanword chapter (pp. 210-211): source-language stress (French) is converted into H tone (non-final syllable) or HL tone (final syllable/monosyllable); and in nominal derivation (p. ~213) where prosodic modification in this language is said to be tonal lowering only.
